title: Month 30
subtitle: Two and a half. The thirty-month visit is this month, and the next one is at three.

baby.development: Your child says three words together, can jump with both feet, and can walk up stairs alternating feet with a hand held. They can name a friend and are starting to take turns.

you.body: If you are pregnant again, thirty months is the gap where the older child can help. Let them.
you.mind: Thirty months is when the child's play gets a plot. It is the best thing to watch, and it is the thing to protect time for.

coreActions.title: Go to the thirty-month visit
coreActions.why: This is a short developmental check, and it is the last visit before the three-year check.
coreActions.detail: The thirty-month visit usually has no vaccines. The doctor will check language, movement, and teeth, and will ask about sleep, eating, and toilet learning. Ask about preschool and about the three-year visit.

coreActions.title: Practise stairs, alternating feet
coreActions.why: Alternating feet on stairs is a thirty-month milestone, and it is built by doing it with a hand held.
coreActions.detail: Walk up and down with a hand held, and say the feet out loud. A child who is still going up one foot at a time at thirty months is not behind, but it is worth practising. Keep the gates until three.

coreActions.title: Give the pretend play a plot
coreActions.why: Pretend play with a sequence is what builds narrative, and narrative is what reading comprehension is made of.
coreActions.detail: Set up a scene: the teddy is sick, the doctor comes, the teddy gets better. Let the child direct. Add one prop, not five. Ask what happens next. This is the work of a two-and-a-half-year-old.

alsoKnow.title: Preschool starts thinking now
alsoKnow.body: Most preschools take children from two and a half or three. Ask about ratios, staff turnover, and how they handle a child who is upset. A visit tells you more than a brochure.

alsoKnow.title: The nap may be ending, but not yet
alsoKnow.body: Most children drop the nap between three and four. A child who is fighting the nap at thirty months is more likely overtired than ready to drop it.

redFlags.text: Choking — cannot breathe, cough, or make a sound
A fever over 100.4°F with unusual sleepiness or a rash
Feeling hopeless, or thoughts of harming yourself or the child
